title: Seven Months at Cromford and Not One Spinning Frame Built
dek: In August 1771 a former wig-maker leased a small Derbyshire stream to drive his spinning machine; by March 1772 not one spinning frame had been made.

story.event: Leasing land and water at Cromford and starting the first water-powered cotton mill
story.summary: On 1 August 1771 Richard Arkwright and his partners, including the hosiers Samuel Need and Jedediah Strutt, leased land and water rights at Cromford in Derbyshire to drive Arkwright's patented roller-spinning machine by water instead of horses. Progress was slow: in March 1772 no frame had been built and skilled workers were hard to find, but the mill was working by 1774 and a second, larger mill followed in 1776-77.
paragraphs: On 1 August 1771, Richard Arkwright and his partners signed a 21-year lease on land and water at Cromford, a lead-mining hamlet in Derbyshire, for £14 a year. Born in Preston, Arkwright had been apprenticed to a barber and had made wigs in Bolton. In 1769 he patented a machine that drew out and spun cotton between pairs of rollers, and he expected horses to drive it.

Two hosiers, Samuel Need of Nottingham and Jedediah Strutt of Derby, had each paid £500 to join him, and a horse-driven mill was being set up in Nottingham. Horses, the partners were finding, were costly and gave too little power. One heritage account says they signed for Cromford before the Nottingham mill had begun production. It was an odd choice: 17 miles from Derby and 44 from Manchester on poor roads, far from the ports that landed raw cotton. It did have a modest brook fed by a lead-mine drain whose water was said never to freeze, mining families whose women and children might take mill work, and distance from rivals keen to copy the machine. Historians can only guess which weighed most.

The start was slow. In December 1771 Arkwright advertised in the Derby Mercury for two journeyman clockmakers, a smith, wood turners, weavers, and women and children. In March 1772, seven months after the lease, he wrote to Strutt that he would be able to make "three frames in a fortnet". Not one had yet been made. The sash windows were not fitted; he asked Strutt to send latches, catches and a large knocker or bell for the front door. Workers he had sent for from Halifax had not come in the numbers he needed. He also resolved to let nobody in to see the works.

The mill was running by 1774, though historians have described its early years as closer to an experimental workshop than a finished factory. Arkwright used that time to mechanise the stages before spinning, patented them in 1775 and built a second, larger mill in 1776-77. A visitor in 1776 counted about 200 children in the first mill, working twelve-hour shifts. Arkwright was knighted in 1786 and became one of the richest men in England, and mills on his pattern spread across Britain and abroad.

quote.text: the man who observes the mean is one who calls a thing by its own name, being truthful both in life and in word, owning to what he has, and neither more nor less.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle praises the person who claims no more than they have. Arkwright promised his partner frames that did not yet exist, while the partner's money sat in an unfinished building. Perhaps that confidence kept the work moving; Aristotle would still call it the wrong measure.

reflection: Seven months in, Arkwright had a building without windows and a promise of three frames a fortnight. Most early work looks like this from the inside: slower than you said, slower than you hoped. The harder part is often not the delay but what you tell people about it.

When someone asks how things are going, a relative, a colleague, someone who has given you their time or trust, it is tempting to describe the version you expect to be true soon. Aristotle's test is plainer: say what is built and what is not yet. It costs a little pride, and it lets everyone, including you on a tired evening, plan around the real state of things.
invitation: Before you next tell anyone how your work is going, write two short lines: what is finished, and what is not yet. Make the second line as plain as the first.

sources.supports: Slow first steps at Cromford: Arkwright's letter to Strutt of March 1772, seven months after the lease, promising 'three frames in a fortnet' when not one frame had been made; sash windows still to be fitted; waiting for latches and door fittings; still recruiting key staff; the mill operational by 1774; pre-spinning processes mechanised 1772-75, second patent 1775, second mill built 1776-77.

sources.title: North Street, Cromford: History Album
sources.supports: Patent granted June 1769; Need and Strutt brought in through the Wright bank; a Nottingham factory of horse-driven frames, horse power proving expensive and insufficient; Cromford's distances (17 miles from Derby, 26 from Nottingham, 44 from Manchester), poor roads and remoteness from ports; reasons for the choice 'can only be conjectured'; Bonsall Brook and Cromford Sough, the Sough water reputed never to freeze; lead miners' families as a labour force; March 1772 letter to Strutt asking for latches, catches and a large knocker or bell and resolving to let no one in to look at the works; lease of 1 August 1771 at £14 a year; text of the Derby Mercury advertisement of 10 December 1771; William Bray's 1776 visit finding 200 children in the first mill on twelve-hour shifts; knighthood in 1786.

sources.title: Out and about in Cromford Mill, Lea Mills and the Lumsdale Valley (The Historian, Autumn 2011)
sources.publisher: The Historical Association (Chris Wrigley, Professor of Modern British History, University of Nottingham)
sources.supports: The 1769 patent specified horse power; Cromford's water did not freeze; first mill established in 1771; labour from lead-mining families; advertisement of 13 December 1771 for two journeymen clockmakers, a smith, two wood turners, weavers, women and children; the first Cromford mill described by Fitton and Wadsworth as more an experimental machine-shop than a properly equipped spinning factory; about 200 people in the first mill; 143 Arkwright-style mills by 1788 and imitators abroad.

cross_checks.claim: Arkwright and his partners took a 21-year lease on land and water at Cromford on 1 August 1771.
Need and Strutt backed Arkwright, and the first mill in Nottingham was to be driven by horses.
In March 1772 Arkwright wrote to Strutt from an unfinished mill, asking for door fittings and struggling to recruit workers.
In December 1771 Arkwright advertised for clockmakers, a smith, wood turners, weavers, women and children.
Building of the first mill began in 1771, it was working by 1774, and a second mill followed in 1776-77.
Arkwright's 1769 patent machine was first meant to be driven by horses, and Cromford's water was reputed not to freeze.

research_notes: Lease date: the Landmark Trust album's introduction says 'In 1770' but its main text, the Derwent Valley Mills Rock House research timeline and a Cromford Mills information sheet all give 1 August 1771 (21 years, £14 a year, from Richard Nall); the Derwent Valley Mills page's 'seven months' before March 1772 also fits August 1771, so the story uses 1 August 1771. Nottingham: the Landmark Trust says a horse-driven factory was set up and horse power proved expensive and too weak; the Derwent Valley Mills Strutt page says the Cromford lease was signed before production began in Nottingham. The story gives both, attributing the second. Advertisement: the Landmark Trust prints it headed 'Cotton Mill, Cromford, 10th Dec. 1771' from the Derby Mercury; Wrigley dates it 13 December 1771 (probably the issue date) and names the paper 'The Daily Mercury', evidently a slip; the story says 'December 1771' and 'Derby Mercury'. Water: the Derbyshire HER links Bonsall Brook and Cromford Sough to the second mill and Wrigley (after Chapman) says the first mill was poorly supplied by Bonsall Brook, while the Derwent Valley Mills page says Arkwright diverted the Sough for the first mill; the story says only 'a modest brook fed by a lead-mine drain', which all accept. Workforce: Wrigley gives about 200 people in the first mill and 450 in the second by 1777; the Landmark Trust cites William Bray's 1776 visit finding 200 children in the first mill on twelve-hour shifts and gives a workforce of 800 by 1777. The story uses only the 1776 visitor's count of about 200 children and does not give a total. The letter: the Derwent Valley Mills Partnership dates it March 1772 and Christie's 2 March 1772; the quotation 'three frames in a fortnet' (Arkwright's spelling) is from the Derwent Valley Mills page; Christie's paraphrases the letter as describing card-setters ordered from Halifax who did not arrive in the right numbers. The 'experimental workshop' description paraphrases Fitton and Wadsworth (1958) as quoted by Wrigley. The Landmark Trust and Historical Association PDFs load but their text is compressed, so the checker cannot see the founder's name in them. Partnership dates (1769 or 1770) and whether John Smalley was still a partner in 1771 differ between sources; the story names only Need and Strutt and says 'his partners'. Wikipedia was not used. Quote: Aristotle is describing the truthful person in social life generally, not commercial promises; it is applied by analogy.
